section_summary: This section consists chiefly of excerpts from monthly U.S. consular reports on Japanese shipping from late 1938 through November 1940, with a reprinted article and a translated ordinance. It traces the shift from voluntary industry controls to government direction of shipbuilding, vessel allocation, freight rates, and cargo priorities. Several reports also list merchant-vessel launches and discuss shipping company finances.

people.name: William C. Affeld Jr.
people.role: American vice consul; report author and approving officer

people.name: Noboru Otani
people.role: President of Nippon Yusen Kaisha; Shipping Control Committee chairman; transportation association chairman

people.name: Shozo Murata
people.role: Shipping association president and later Minister of Communications

people.name: Katsumi Yamagata
people.role: Tatsuuma Shipping Company representative and shipping-control plan proponent

people.name: Shigeru Hata
people.role: Managing director of the Central Shipping Transportation Control Association

people.name: Toshio Koharu
people.role: Managing director of Osaka Shosen Kaisha

people.name: Taro Yamashita
people.role: Managing director of Yamashita Kisen Kaisha

subfiles.title: Shipping administration bureau proposal, concluding page
subfiles.about: A proposed Communications Ministry bureau would divide control, marine affairs, and shipping work among three divisions.
subfiles.summary: Concludes a proposal for a new wartime shipping bureau.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During October 1938
subfiles.from: William C. Affeld Jr., American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports two vessel launches and Kokusai Kisen Kaisha’s financial recovery.
subfiles.summary: Lists October merchant-vessel launches and describes Kokusai Kisen Kaisha’s improved profits, debt restructuring, and possible resumption of dividends.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During November 1938
subfiles.from: William E. Yuni, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reviews Nippon Yusen Kaisha’s six percent dividend and reduced earnings.
subfiles.summary: Explains the company’s lower profits and its president’s views on trade conditions, costs, and voluntary regulation of coastal freight rates.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During December 1938
subfiles.from: William C. Affeld Jr., American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Lists vessel launches and describes proposed statutory controls over shipping associations.
subfiles.summary: The report records December launches and negotiations over legislation giving legal force to existing industry controls. It describes compulsory association membership and a planned Kobe federation empowered to manage rates and tonnage.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During February 1939
subfiles.from: William C. Affeld Jr., American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Assesses the progress and opposition facing several shipping bills.
subfiles.summary: Discusses disputes over seamen’s insurance, ship financing, and the Shipping Association Act, whose draft would place shipping activities under ministerial control.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During March 1939
subfiles.from: William C. Affeld Jr., American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports passage of shipping, shipbuilding, financing, and seamen’s insurance laws.
subfiles.summary: Outlines five recently passed laws, expected implementation dates, licensing of shipbuilding, and expanded credit for new vessels.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During April 1939
subfiles.from: William C. Affeld Jr., American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Lists vessel launches and examines rising pressure for direct government control of shipping.
subfiles.summary: The report connects vessel shortages and high charter rates with government consideration of compulsory ship assignment. It notes efforts to secure transport for essential imports, Army rate reductions, and new restrictions on corporate dividends.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During May 1939
subfiles.from: William C. Affeld Jr., American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Lists launches and compares industry and ministry plans for shipping control.
subfiles.summary: After listing May launches, the report describes the rejection of an industry voluntary-control plan as too weak. A ministry proposal would place a government-business council over existing bodies to direct tonnage toward vital cargoes.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During June 1939
subfiles.from: William C. Affeld Jr., American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Describes negotiations over a proposed Ship Control Council.
subfiles.summary: Shipping interests proposed a council to allocate tonnage, review contracts, and compensate operators for compulsory assignments; ministry acceptance remained uncertain.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During July 1939
subfiles.from: William E. Yuni, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Surveys proposed controls and overseas tramp-shipping concerns.
subfiles.summary: Reports plans to direct vessel distribution and prioritize essential cargoes, submission of an industry council proposal, rejection of a separate Shipping Ministry, and shipowners’ fears of losing overseas tramp business.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During August 1939
subfiles.from: William E. Yuni, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Explains the Cabinet-approved plan for shipping and shipbuilding control commissions.
subfiles.summary: The Cabinet approved a plan to regulate ship construction, cargo contracts, vessel allocation, and freight and charter rates. Mixed official-industry commissions would administer the controls.

subfiles.title: Control of Ocean Freight Rates
subfiles.from: The Oriental Economist
subfiles.about: Analyzes freight costs and proposals to control Japanese ocean transport.
subfiles.summary: The article compares freight charges across iron ore, coal, salt, lumber, and other imports, emphasizing the high cost of tramp service. It links rising rates to vessel shortages and construction costs, then describes proposed rate controls, cargo priorities, and greater oversight of shipyards.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During December 1939
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Lists commercial vessels launched by mid-December 1939.
subfiles.summary: Records vessel names, tonnages, speeds, shipyards, and owners.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During February 1940
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Explains the new Marine Transportation Control Ordinance and possible compulsory ship allocation.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance gives the government broad powers over shipbuilding, repairs, routes, cargoes, rates, and charters. The report considers compulsory allocation to move essential goods despite operators’ reluctance to accept less profitable services.

subfiles.title: Marine Transportation (Shipping) Control Ordinance
subfiles.from: Japanese government
subfiles.about: Sets out legal powers to regulate Japanese vessel construction and marine transport.
subfiles.summary: The translated ordinance requires construction permits and authorizes directions concerning repairs, vessel use, charters, navigation, cargo handling, prices, and rates. It provides for compensation, reporting, inspections, and delegated administration. Its additional rules specify implementation dates in Japan and colonial territories.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During April 1940
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Discusses a new shipping association and a proposed common vessel-charter company.
subfiles.summary: The report anticipates a government-backed association controlling large vessels and describes a proposed joint company to acquire and charter ships. Wartime conditions and limited foreign vessels constrain purchases.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During May 1940
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports the inauguration and leadership of the Nippon Shipping Society.
subfiles.summary: The new society replaced the Japan Shipowners Association and was charged with controlling owners of vessels over 1,000 tons.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During June 1940
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports proposals to tighten vessel and cargo allocation.
subfiles.summary: The ministry considered a ship-assignment council and use of ordinance powers to charter idle vessels and restrict routes and cargoes.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During July 1940
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Examines vessel shortages and proposals for stronger shipping controls.
subfiles.summary: The report describes shortcomings in existing control bodies and shortages affecting essential cargoes. Proposals include compulsory vessel distribution, tighter supervision of distant routes, joint cargo collection, and a profit-equalization fund.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During August 1940
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Compares industry and government proposals for expanded shipping control.
subfiles.summary: Shipowners proposed a mixed commission to allocate cargoes and manage rates, while the ministry favored direct authority over vessel and freight-space allocation. The report also describes growing support for pooling routes, vessels, warehouses, and profits.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During September 1940
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Describes the announced structure of Japan’s revised shipping-control system.
subfiles.summary: A government inquiry council would plan allocations, the Communications Ministry would issue binding orders, and industry bodies would administer ship assignment and rates. The plan sought to pool shipping resources across vessel types.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During October 1940
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Details the roles and proposed membership of two shipping-control bodies.
subfiles.summary: The Shipping Control Committee would retain authority over rates, fees, and compensation while vessel assignment would pass to a central transport association. The report describes proposed divisions by vessel type and route, participation from Korea and Kwantung, and calls for a shippers’ association to coordinate cargoes.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During November 1940
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports the inauguration of the Central Shipping Transportation Control Association.
subfiles.summary: The association began work with 95 member companies, although full tonnage allocation was expected later. The excerpt names its officers and describes plans to approve transport contracts and give essential cargoes priority. The report continues beyond page 400.
